claims.text: As-cast HfNbTiVAl10 has a hierarchical heterostructure containing multiple heterogeneously distributed phase regions.
As-cast HfNbTiVAl10 exhibits associated lattice distortions.
The hierarchical microstructure includes coherent interfaces.
Heterogeneously distributed phases and coherent interfaces mediate dislocation motion and strain localization.
A machine-learning surrogate can use measured phase fractions, misfit volumes, lattice-distortion parameters, and precipitate characteristics as predictive inputs.
The surrogate can predict Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture behavior of as-cast HfNbTiVAl10.
The surrogate will be approximately ten times faster than established DFT or atomistic simulations.
Predictions of all three target properties will agree with experimental measurements within a 15–20% error margin.
The surrogate will improve predictive accuracy relative to baseline DFT-based or atomistic methods.
Conventional DFT and atomistic simulations require extensive computational time and resources for this alloy's elastic and fracture responses.
Phase distribution and other casting- or processing-dependent microstructural variations affect the predictability of mechanical response.
Solid-solution strengthening, precipitation strengthening, and interfacial load transfer govern Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture behavior in HfNbTiVAl10.
Room-temperature testing at a strain rate near 10^-3 s^-1 is an appropriate declared validation condition.
SEM and TEM measurements will be used to validate the model's microstructural descriptors.
The approach may fail when relevant microstructural features are inadequately characterized.
Unexpected phase segregation or nanoscale defects omitted from the descriptors may dominate mechanical response and cause model failure.
Descriptor generalization across different processing conditions is uncertain.
Strain-rate changes may introduce nonlinear effects not represented by the model.
Consistent deviations greater than 20% across multiple independent tests would falsify the hypothesis.
